# draw — layered drawings and animations

A drawing is `{"job": {...}, "scene": {...}}`. The **job** says canvas, frame
count, timing and views; the **scene** says what is drawn: layers (back to
front), and per view the parts cut from the source sprite, the nodes that draw
them, and how nodes move per frame.

## Complete example — raise and wave the right arm, with a sparkle

For a 48x48 south-facing character whose right arm (screen right) occupies
source pixels `[34,20]..[41,33]`, shoulder at `[35,21]`:

```json
{
  "job": {
    "canvas": [64, 64],
    "frame_count": 4,
    "durations_ms": [160, 120, 160, 120],
    "views": [{"id": "south", "offset": [8, 8]}]
  },
  "scene": {
    "palette": {"spark": "#fff7dc"},
    "layers": [
      {"id": "body", "name": "Body - base"},
      {"id": "arm", "name": "Body - right arm"},
      {"id": "fx", "name": "VFX - sparkle"}
    ],
    "views": {
      "south": {
        "selections": {
          "arm": {"regions": [[34, 20, 41, 33]]},
          "rest": {}
        },
        "nodes": {
          "root": {"layer": "body", "draw": [], "at": [8, 8]},
          "body": {"layer": "body", "draw": [{"op": "copy", "part": "rest"}],
                   "at": {"node": "root", "point": [0, 0]}},
          "arm": {"layer": "arm", "draw": [{"op": "copy", "part": "arm"}],
                  "at": {"node": "root", "point": [0, 0]}, "pivot": [35, 21]},
          "spark": {"layer": "fx", "visible": false,
                    "at": {"node": "arm", "point": [38, 34]},
                    "draw": [{"op": "brush", "points": [[-2, 0], [2, 0]], "color": "spark"},
                             {"op": "brush", "points": [[0, -2], [0, 2]], "color": "spark"}]}
        },
        "tracks": [
          {"node": "root", "property": "at", "interpolation": "step",
           "keys": [[1, [8, 8]], [3, [8, 7]]]},
          {"node": "arm", "property": "angle", "keys": [[1, 0], [2, -90], [3, -150], [4, -90]]},
          {"node": "spark", "property": "visible", "interpolation": "step",
           "keys": [[1, false], [3, true], [4, false]]}
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Call it with the sprite: `draw --recipe '<the JSON above>' --sources '{"south": "character:<id>:south"}'` — as argv items, `["draw", "--recipe", <json>, "--sources", <json>]` (any single-frame image reference works as a source).

How to read it:
- **Coordinates.** A part keeps its source coordinates. A node's `at` is where
  its local `[0,0]` lands on the canvas, so a part drawn by a node at the view's
  `offset` sits exactly where the source does. The `root` node carries the whole
  body; children anchor to it with `{"node": "root", "point": [0, 0]}` and move
  with it.
- **Selections** cut the source: each visible pixel belongs to the
  FIRST selection that matches it (`regions` rectangles and/or exact `colors`);
  an empty `{}` last takes the remainder. Every part must contain pixels.
- **Tracks** set a node property per frame: `at`, `pivot`, `angle` (degrees,
  clockwise on screen — negative raises a right arm outward), `opacity` (0-255),
  `visible` (step only). Keys are `[frame, value]`, cyclic: frame 4 blends back
  toward frame 1. A track with `"anchor": "root"` makes `at` relative to that node.
- **Anchors follow**: the spark is anchored to a point on the arm, so it rides the
  rotation.

## Explicit poses instead of tracks

Two independent choices per view: how the source is cut — `selections` or
`parts` (polygon masks) — and how it is timed — `tracks`, or `poses` with
`frames`. Mix them freely, one of each; giving both forms of one choice is
refused. The same view with parts and poses:

```json
"south": {
  "parts": {
    "arm":  {"include": [[[34, 20], [42, 20], [42, 34], [34, 34]]]},
    "rest": {"exclude": [[[34, 20], [42, 20], [42, 34], [34, 34]]]}
  },
  "nodes": { "...": "same as above" },
  "poses": {"rest": {}, "up": {"arm": {"angle": -150}, "spark": {"visible": true}}},
  "frames": ["rest", "up", "up", "rest"]
}
```

A pose overrides node fields for the frames that name it; `draw` in a pose
replaces that node's whole command list for those frames (redraw a hand, open an
eye). Polygon masks use pixel-corner coordinates: `[[34,20],[42,20],[42,34],[34,34]]`
covers pixels 34..41 x 20..33.

## Job fields

Required: `canvas` `[w, h]`, `frame_count`, `views`.
Defaults: `durations_ms` 100 each (10 ms steps), `columns`, `body_prefix`
`"Body"`, `overview_scale` (review zoom). The server fills every path/hash field.

- `views`: `[{"id": "south", "offset": [x, y]}]`; add `{"id": "west",
  "mirror_of": "east"}` for a horizontally mirrored view (no scene data needed).
  Optional `protected_regions`: `[{"name": "face", "region": [x0,y0,x1,y1],
  "mode": "source_pixels" | "exact"}]` — checked on every body frame.
- `source_bookends_exact` (default true): frame 1's body must equal the source
  at its offset. Set false when drawing from scratch or restyling every frame.
  `return_to_rest: true` also checks the last frame.
- `body_palette_exact`: body frames may only use source colours.
- `require_clear_border`: fail if any frame touches the canvas edge.
- `events`: named frames, e.g. `{"impact": 6}` (reported back, for game code).
- `gif_background`: opaque matte for the GIF preview when the art has partial
  alpha (the server picks one if you don't).
- `changes`: revision operations (see `describe animation`); normally
  appended via `draw --drawing <id> --changes '[…]'`.

## Drawing commands (in a node's `draw`)

`copy` (part, optional `region`, `method: "nearest"|"scale2x8"`), `rect` / `ellipse`
(`box`), `circle` (`center`, `radius`), `polygon` / `path` (`points`), `brush`
(`points`, `size`, `shape`), `pixels` (`[[x, y, colour], ...]`), `grid` (below).
Shapes take `color`, optional `fill: false`, `outline`, `stroke_width`. Colours
may be palette names. Full reference: `describe scenes`.

`grid` writes pixels as text, one character per pixel — the way to draw faces,
gems and other small details: `{"op": "grid", "at": [8, 12], "legend": {"o":
"ink", "w": "white"}, "rows": ["..oo..", ".owwo.", "..oo.."]}`. `.` (or a space)
is a transparent cell, as in `crop`'s rows: it clears the pixel under it, or
with `"mode": "stamp"` leaves that pixel as it is.

To fix pixels in something already drawn, `crop <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1`
(inclusive corners) prints them as rows with a legend, plus the `paste` call that
writes them back: edit the rows in that call and run it. The pixels go into the
named node's own drawing, so they move with it on every frame — except where the
node is clipped, rotated or anchored: there they are fixed to the canvas on the
cropped frame only (the reply counts them as layer patches). Its `--expect`
fingerprint refuses the paste if those pixels changed since the crop.

## What goes wrong, and how to see it

- **Half pixels.** Linear position keys land between pixels and shift parts
  unevenly. Give positions integer values with `"interpolation": "step"`, or a
  key on every frame. Angles and opacity interpolate fine.
- **Rotation.** 90° steps are exact; other angles resample the cutout. Keep
  rotated parts small, rotate around a joint (`pivot`), and zoom on the joint.
  `"method": "scale2x8"` on the copy can give cleaner rotated edges.
- **Revealed gaps.** Moving a part exposes what it covered (torso behind an
  arm, a missing shoulder). Draw the hidden surface on a layer beneath it
  (`circle`/`polygon`/`pixels` in the sprite's own colours), then check at 10x.
- **Carried pixels.** A rectangle selection can take a few pixels of cloth or
  outline from a neighbour. Look at the body-only sheet in motion frames.
- **Room.** Motion and effects need canvas margin; the sprite never scales.
- **Order.** Layers draw back to front; nodes within one layer in JSON order.
- **Body vs effects.** Name body layers `Body - …` and effects anything else:
  the body-only sheet lets you judge the motion without the effects on top.
- **From scratch.** Omit the view's source (you get a transparent canvas of the
  full size at offset `[0,0]`) and set `source_bookends_exact: false`. A still
  drawing needs no `tracks`, `poses` or `selections` — just `nodes`.

After the first render, fix things with small `changes` (`set_node` moves or
redraws a node on chosen frames; pixel operations touch individual layer
pixels) rather than rewriting the recipe — the response then shows a before/after
against the previous render.
